groups.content:
The White Sands footprints

Dating the footprints

  • Researchers dug a [8] next to the prints.
  • They dated seeds of ditch [9] found above and below the prints.
  • To answer critics, they also dated pollen from [10] trees.
  • Grains of [11] were dated by finding when they were last exposed to sunlight.

What the footprints show

  • Most were made by teenagers and [12].
  • No stone [13] have been found at the site, so it is hard to identify the people.

Questions 35-40

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

In boxes 35-40 on your answer sheet, write

YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.explanation: Answer: FALSE Paragraph 2: ' in the late 2000s a park ranger recognised the first human footprints there ', long before the 2021 announcement.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 2: ghost tracks ' are invisible for most of the year and appear only briefly ' when the moisture is right.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 3 says ditch grass 'had grown along the edge of the lake' in the past, but says nothing about whether it still grows in the area today.

Answer: FALSE Paragraph 4: the dominant view was about 13,000 years ago, ' Later discoveries pushed this date back to around 16,000 years ago ', and 'few researchers had seriously considered' an earlier date.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 6: ' the researchers returned to the site and tested two completely different materials ', pollen and quartz, dated by different techniques.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 7 says most prints 'appear to have been made by teenagers and children', but nothing is said about whether the researchers found this surprising.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 7: sloth prints show the animal rising up and turning, ' possibly in response to people who were following it '.
Answer: trench Paragraph 3: 'the researchers dug a trench beside them and examined the layers of sediment'.
Answer: grass Paragraph 3: 'they found thousands of seeds from ditch grass , an aquatic plant'.
Answer: conifer Paragraph 6: 'The first was pollen from conifer trees, which take their carbon from the air'.
Answer: quartz Paragraph 6: 'The second was grains of quartz , which were dated using a technique that measures when the grains were last exposed to sunlight.'
Answer: children Paragraph 7: 'Most of them appear to have been made by teenagers and children '.
Answer: tools Paragraph 8: 'So far, no stone tools have been found alongside the White Sands footprints, which makes it harder to identify who these people were.'
Answer: G Paragraph G: ' protecting seagrass must go hand in hand with supporting the people who use the coast ', and local people who 'can see that healthy meadows mean more fish' defend them.
Answer: A Paragraph A: ' around a third of the world's seagrass has been lost since the late nineteenth century'. The 'fifth' in D refers to fisheries, not losses.
Answer: H Paragraph H: 'there are signs that attitudes are changing', and ' Now people are starting to understand that it matters. '
Answer: B Paragraph B describes traditional uses (mattresses, insulation, roofs) and says ' these meadows are part of local history and identity '.
Answer: carbon Paragraph C: meadows 'are also remarkably effective at storing carbon , much of which is locked away in the sediment'.
Answer: nurseries Paragraph D: 'many commercially important species of fish use the meadows as nurseries , spending the early part of their lives there'.
Answer: algae Paragraph E: 'the extra nutrients encourage the rapid growth of algae , which block the sunlight that seagrass needs'.
Answer: sediment Paragraph E: when the plants die, ' sediment is released into the water, making it even cloudier'.
Answer: chains Paragraph E: moorings are attached to buoys by chains, and 'as boats swing with the wind and tide, the chains scrape away circles of seagrass'.

Answer: A (Helen Frost) Paragraph G: Frost believes projects succeed only when local people are fully involved: ' If fishing communities and boat owners are part of the decision-making ... they become the meadows' strongest defenders'.
Answer: C (Rafael Ortega) Paragraph H: ' Some countries have made seagrass protection a priority, while others have barely begun to think about it ,' says Ortega.
Answer: D (Grace Whitlow) Paragraph F: Whitlow believes most damage is not intentional: ' I've never met anyone who wanted to harm seagrass '.
Answer: B (Tom Aldous) Paragraph C: restoration 'does not require expensive technology': volunteers collect and plant seeds by hand. ' It's slow work, but it isn't complicated. '

text.en: The writer felt uncomfortable for the whole journey.
Hartmann had designed the car they were travelling in.
The weather caused the car to drive dangerously.
Certain situations on the road caused the car to hesitate.

questions.explanation: Answer: D When a van stops, ' the car pauses for a long time, apparently unsure ', and at road works 'it slows almost to a stop'. The writer begins to relax (A), nothing says Hartmann designed the car (B), and the car is cautious rather than dangerous (C).

text.en: the fact that it always follows the same route
the small number of passengers it carries
the support of the university authorities

questions.explanation: Answer: A The shuttle 'follows exactly the same path every day', and ' That predictability is what makes it possible '.

text.en: the public showed little interest in driverless cars at the time.
radio was a promising technology for guiding vehicles.
predictions about driverless cars have often been too optimistic.
car manufacturers were the first to invest seriously in automation.

questions.explanation: Answer: C The exhibition predicted automated motorways 'by around 1960', and ' Similar predictions have been made in almost every decade since ', while the subtitle notes they have been promised 'within ten years' for decades. The exhibition was 'popular' (A), and serious investment came from technology companies (D).

text.en: People will soon get used to it.
People's reluctance to do it is understandable.
It will reduce the cost of travel for everyone.
Companies have now found a solution to the problem.

questions.explanation: Answer: B After Ferreira says people are uncomfortable sharing, the writer comments: ' That can hardly have come as a surprise. ' Whether sharing becomes normal 'will depend on how widely the technology is adopted' (A, D).
Answer: C Services 'have expanded particularly rapidly in China', but ' Even there, however, the technology has significant limitations. '
Answer: E ' They cope well with unexpected situations because they can draw on years of experience of how other people behave.'
Answer: F A driverless car 'must find other ways to show its intentions', and ' it must also follow local driving customs , which vary widely'.
Answer: B ' Because each vehicle's software can be adjusted for the place where it operates , driverless cars might actually help to preserve these regional habits'.
Answer: NO ' Professional drivers are unlikely to regard it as progress , and many are already campaigning against it.'
Answer: YES ' Whether driverless cars will make ordinary people's daily lives better is also still an open question. '
Answer: NO The writer says the opposite: driverless cars could let older people go out ' without depending on relatives, allowing them to remain independent for longer '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer discusses what may be lost for people who enjoy driving, but says nothing about driving tests.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer says 'Many people enjoy driving for its own sake', but gives no information about what kind of cars they prefer.
Answer: YES Final paragraph: ' the reasons people drive have never been purely practical ', and the pleasure of driving will survive.
